ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The diagram shows a liquid in an open beaker/container, with a wavy liquid surface exposed at the top. The solution contains dissolved ions labeled K+, NO3-, and Ag+. At the bottom there is a solid precipitate mound labeled Ag2SO4. Reasoning: If the beaker is left uncovered for several hours, some water solvent can evaporate, but the dissolved ions and existing solid salt do not evaporate. Evaporation decreases the amount of solvent and increases the concentrations of Ag+ and SO4^2- species in the remaining solution. Because silver sulfate, Ag2SO4, is only slightly soluble and is already present as a precipitate, the more concentrated solution will exceed its solubility balance and deposit more Ag2SO4 as solid.

Image description: The beaker contains a liquid with dissolved ions labeled K⁺, NO₃⁻, and Ag⁺. At the bottom of the beaker there is a solid deposit labeled Ag₂SO₄, showing that silver sulfate has already precipitated.

Reasoning: Since solid Ag₂SO₄ is present in contact with solution, the system can be treated as a saturated silver sulfate equilibrium: Ag₂SO₄(s) ⇌ 2 Ag⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq). If the uncovered beaker sits for several hours, water evaporates. Evaporation reduces the amount of solvent and tends to increase the ion concentrations in solution, making the ion product exceed Ksp. To restore the solubility-product equilibrium, the system shifts toward forming more solid Ag₂SO₄.
